claims.text: Increasing the aluminum content of the refractory AlNbTiVZr-based alloy by approximately 5–10 at.% will promote formation of a continuous, adherent alumina scale.
The resulting alumina scale will improve high-temperature oxygen resistance relative to the untreated alloy.
The unmodified baseline alloy develops non-protective, spalling oxide scales at high temperatures.
An aluminum increase of 5–10 at.% is a modest modification.
The proposed oxidation-resistance improvement should occur in static laboratory air at approximately 800 °C for 100 hours.
The modified alloy will form an ultrathin alumina layer that is continuous and adherent.
Added aluminum will oxidize preferentially at high temperature to form alumina.
The alumina scale will be slow-growing and act as a diffusion barrier to oxygen ingress.
Retarding oxygen ingress will limit scale spallation and reduce overall oxidation kinetics.
The increased-aluminum alloy will have a significantly lower mass gain than the untreated alloy after the specified exposure.
The increased-aluminum alloy will have a more uniform and adherent alumina layer than the untreated alloy.
At 800 °C, the untreated alloy exhibits two-stage oxidation kinetics consisting of initial parabolic behavior followed by breakaway oxidation.
The untreated AlNbTiVZr 0.25 alloy gains approximately 107.5 mg/cm² after 100 hours in static air at 800 °C.
The untreated alloy has a non-uniform oxide scale after the specified exposure.
The efficacy of added aluminum at higher temperatures, under cyclic thermal exposure, or in more aggressive oxidizing atmospheres is uncertain.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant mass-gain reduction, a continuous adherent alumina scale, or oxidation kinetics different from the baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
